welcome.card: Funding sources, proposals, budgets, and letters of inquiry for nonprofit clients.
welcome.intro: Funders don't fund good intentions. They fund clear needs, measurable outcomes, and budgets where every dollar has a job. PVV's financial team helps clients find funding and write grant materials, and this training walks you through that process with one practice client.
welcome.outcome: A funder shortlist, a need statement, SMART outcomes, a checked line-item budget, and the opening of a letter of inquiry, all built for a practice client.

modules.title: Two doors of funding

blocks.x: Under PVV's constitution, the financial team assists nonprofits in writing grants. Before you touch a single application, learn the most common mistake new members make: confusing money for PVV with money for clients. They are different applications, different accounts, and different rules.

blocks.caption: Door 1 keeps PVV running. Door 2 is what you help clients pursue.

blocks.x: The PVV Treasurer manages the club's budget and makes sure operational grants like Haas Transportation Grants and Haas Center Event Co-Sponsorship are applied for. Amounts and deadlines change, so ask the Treasurer for current numbers. Your category chair directs the client grant work.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.x: PVV advises on Door 2. The client's executive director signs and submits. Our name is not on the application.

modules.title: Find funders that fit

blocks.x: The goal of prospecting is fit, not volume. Sending one generic proposal to a long list of funders doesn't work. A short list of funders who already care about your client's work and place does.

blocks.title: The fit check
blocks.x: Does the funder support this location, this cause, and this size of request? Is the client eligible, for example as a 501(c)(3)? What is the deadline? Who have they funded before?

modules.title: Anatomy of a proposal

blocks.x: Most grant proposals want the same things in different words. Candid's introductory material lists the typical parts, and learning them lets you read any funder's guidelines quickly.

head: Section
What it answers
rows: Who are you, what do you need, and why does it matter?
What specific problem exists, and how big is it?
What will you do, and how?
What will change, and how will you measure it?
Why are you the right group to do this?
What does it cost, and where does the money come from?

head: Vague
SMART
rows: 80% of 30 students improve at least one grade level in math by June
Serve 200 families a month with weekly groceries for 12 months

blocks.x: Data: in [community], [X]% experience [problem]. Story: one person, with permission. Consequence: without help, [what happens]. Your angle: [org] is positioned to help because [evidence].

modules.title: Budgets funders trust

blocks.x: Many funders read the budget before the narrative, and they check that the two agree. A budget describes the project in numbers the same way the proposal describes it in words.

head: Category
Examples
rows: Insurance, office supplies. Many funders cap this, so check each funder's rules.
Donated goods and volunteer time, valued at a published rate

blocks.title: Golden rule
blocks.x: If the narrative says "serve 45 students twice a week," the budget must show the staff hours and supplies for exactly that. Reviewers check.
For volunteer time, the standard is Independent Sector's annual estimate. For 2026 it is $36.14 per hour nationally, with a different figure for each state.

blocks.title: Candid: What do funders look for in grant proposal budgets?
blocks.why: Funders' own view of what makes a budget credible.

blocks.title: Candid: examples of nonprofit budgets
blocks.why: Skim the difference between direct and indirect costs and what counts as in-kind.

blocks.title: Do the math
blocks.intro: A tutoring program serves 30 students, 2 sessions a week, for 36 weeks. Each student needs a $35 workbook. The coordinator works 15 hours a week at $20 an hour. The grant is $12,000, and the funder caps administrative costs at 10%. Enter numbers only.

fields.label: Total coordinator cost for the 36 weeks
Maximum administrative costs on the $12,000 grant
Value of 100 volunteer hours at $36.14 an hour

blocks.q: A budget says "$10,000 for supplies" with no breakdown. What does a funder think?
options: It looks suspicious. They want itemized calculations.
blocks.explain: Itemizing shows you've planned the project and makes the budget checkable.

blocks.q: Which rate should you use to value volunteer time as an in-kind match?
options: Independent Sector's published rate, nationally or for your state
blocks.explain: It's the standard funders recognize, and it's updated every April.

modules.title: Narrative and letter of inquiry

blocks.x: Many funders ask for a letter of inquiry (LOI) before a full proposal. It's a short letter that introduces your client and the request, and it decides whether you're invited to apply. Treat it as your best two minutes.

head: Part
Job
rows: Who the client is and what you are asking for, in one or two sentences
The total request, and a thank-you

blocks.title: Always follow the funder's guidelines
blocks.x: Length, format, and questions vary. Candid's examples of green flags include tailoring the proposal to the funder and answering each question clearly. Never send the same letter to every funder.

blocks.title: Candid sample documents: letters of inquiry
blocks.why: Open one sample letter of inquiry and notice how short it is.

fields.label: Write a five-sentence LOI opening for the practice pantry: who we are, the need, the ask, the outcome, and the amount.
Which of the funder's stated priorities does your letter echo?

blocks.q: A funder's guidelines say "no more than one page." Your LOI is a page and a half. What do you do?
blocks.explain: Following the guidelines is the first thing reviewers check.
blocks.hint: What do guidelines signal about the reviewer?

blocks.q: Which is a green flag for a funder?
options: One proposal sent unchanged to 50 funders
A proposal tailored to the funder that answers each question clearly
blocks.explain: Tailoring shows you read their priorities.

checklist: I wrote an LOI opening that includes the ask and amount
I know to follow each funder's guidelines
I tailored the letter to a specific funder's priorities

modules.title: Track, comply, and stay in scope

blocks.x: Grants run on deadlines and follow-up. A funding tracker keeps the client from missing either, and it's what a new liaison reads first when taking over.

head: Tracker column
Example
rows: A date, with a reminder two weeks earlier

items: PVV advises and drafts. The client decides, signs, and submits.
No legal or tax advice. If a client asks whether they qualify as a 501(c)(3), point them to their board or accountant.
Keep client financial information in the client's accounts, not your personal ones.
Beyond grants, PVV also helps clients navigate benefits and connect to available resources. Ask your chair before taking on anything new.

blocks.intro: Combine your work into one Google Doc or Sheet: funder shortlist, need statement, outcomes, the budget math, and your LOI opening. Set sharing to Anyone with the link can view, then paste the link. Your category chair will review it.

blocks.q: A client asks whether their organization qualifies for 501(c)(3) status. What do you say?
options: PVV can't give legal or tax advice. Please check with your board or an accountant.
blocks.explain: Legal and tax questions go to qualified professionals.

blocks.q: A funder declines the proposal. What is the best next step?

blocks.explain: Feedback strengthens the next application and the relationship.
